opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing I value most is that nobody on the team gets to grade their own homework in isolation.

When you're building models for molecular structure and drug discovery, it's very easy to fool yourself. An ML person can look at a benchmark, see the number go up, and feel great about it. But a structural biologist might look at the same predictions and say, "That binding pose is physically implausible," or "This test set overlaps heavily with what you trained on, so of course it looks good." And a medicinal chemist might say, "Even if this is right, it doesn't help me make a decision I actually care about."

Having those people in the same room, and in the same conversations from the start, changes the questions you ask. Instead of "how do we score on this leaderboard," it becomes "would a scientist trust this enough to spend real lab time and money acting on it?" That's a much harder bar, and a much more honest one.

There's also a healthy tension in it. The ML folks push on scale, generalization, and what the model could do in principle. The wet-lab and domain people keep pulling it back to messy reality: noisy assays, weird edge cases, targets that don't look like anything in the training data. You need both. If you only have the first, you overclaim. If you only have the second, you never take the big swings.

So for me, the cross-disciplinary part isn't a nice-to-have. It's basically the evaluation methodology. Different experts are skeptical in different ways, and a model that survives all of those kinds of skepticism is one you can actually believe in.

fable-5.1.text:
I value that no result at Chai gets to stand on its own. The machine learning side wants a clean held-out test set and a single score. The experimental scientists sitting next to them ask the harder questions: is this a target anyone has actually drugged, does this binder look chemically sensible, does the fold hold up in an assay rather than just in a viewer.

That tension keeps us honest. A benchmark win means one thing, but what we really care about is whether a prediction survives contact with the lab. The cross-disciplinary team turns abstract capability claims into something testable, and that's what tells us what the models can really do.

astra-6.text:
What I value is having people who look at the same model behavior and ask different questions. From an engineering perspective, you might ask whether a result is reproducible. Someone else might ask whether it actually makes for a better conversation, or whether we’re reading more understanding into the response than is really there.

That mix helps you challenge your own assumptions. A model can look impressive in a few examples, but figuring out what it can reliably do takes multiple perspectives—and a willingness to investigate where those perspectives disagree.
